review_method: Focused reading of full-text methods, results, discussion and conclusions; findings are approved only for the narrowly stated claim.

reviews.population: Endurance athletes in 14 included studies; only two running studies among several sports.
reviews.finding: Overreaching protocols were associated with a small reduction in actigraphic sleep efficiency (mean difference -2.0 percentage points, 95% CI -3.2 to -0.8) across three objectively measured studies. Subjective sleep quality did not show a clear effect.
reviews.limitations: High risk of bias, only three objective sleep studies, and no polysomnography. A normal training week or a single short night cannot be labeled overreaching from these results.
reviews.approved_use: Context for a future sustained high-training plus sleep-change insight, with caution; never infer overreaching from Garmin sleep duration alone.

reviews.population: Umbrella review of 24 systematic reviews covering multiple consumer wearable brands and outcomes.
reviews.finding: Wearable sleep estimates often overestimated total sleep time and sleep efficiency compared with reference standards; validity varied by device and measure.
reviews.limitations: The synthesis lags new hardware and software, and its aggregate results do not validate or invalidate a particular Garmin model. It cannot supply a personal error correction factor.
reviews.approved_use: Explain measurement uncertainty when showing sleep trends; avoid treating sleep stages or small nightly changes as exact.

reviews.population: Trials comparing HRV-guided with predefined endurance training in healthy adults of varied training status.
reviews.finding: HRV-guided training improved some vagal-related HRV measures, but pooled differences in aerobic fitness and endurance performance were small and not statistically significant.
reviews.limitations: Few studies, varied HRV indices and recording methods, and limited subgroup power. Overnight consumer HRV is not interchangeable with every protocol in the reviewed trials.
reviews.approved_use: Explain why an isolated low HRV reading should be interpreted with sleep, symptoms and recent training, rather than dictate a workout.

reviews.population: Umbrella review of 13 reviews of running-related injury risk factors.
reviews.finding: Injury associations involve training, health, lifestyle, morphology and biomechanics, with heterogeneous definitions and populations.
reviews.limitations: All included reviews were rated low or critically low quality; no single weekly-volume change can be used as a reliable personal injury prediction.
reviews.approved_use: Caution against labeling a larger running week as an injury forecast.

reviews.population: Middle- and long-distance runners across training levels in controlled strength-training studies.
reviews.finding: High-load and plyometric strength training were associated with improved laboratory running economy in the meta-analysis; effects varied by method and tested speed.
reviews.limitations: Running economy is not the same as race performance. Many tests used absolute rather than athlete-relative speeds, and some method subgroups had few studies.
reviews.approved_use: Context for a future strength-training trend; do not infer that a particular user gained economy from counting strength sessions.

reviews.population: Twenty-seven heterogeneous studies, largely across sports rather than runners alone.
reviews.finding: The review found associations between some acute:chronic workload ratios and injury, but definitions, loads and reference groups varied enough to prevent a stable pooled estimate.
reviews.limitations: Potential search and publication bias, no pooled meta-analysis, and limited transferability to an individual runner. No threshold should be presented as a safe zone.
reviews.approved_use: Support a decision to avoid an injury-risk score based solely on an acute:chronic ratio.

reviews.population: Prospective Garmin-RUNSAFE cohort of recreational runners followed for up to 18 months.
reviews.finding: Reported injury occurrence differed by running experience, weekly frequency, weekly distance and structured-program participation.
reviews.limitations: Observational baseline group comparisons cannot show that increasing frequency or distance will reduce an individual runner’s injury risk. Some groups were small.
reviews.approved_use: Context for why a simple mileage-spike warning must consider training history and other factors; do not recommend a 25 km/week target.
